questions.question: A reversible heat engine has efficiency \( 20\% \). If it is run in reverse as a refrigerator between the same reservoirs, its coefficient of performance is:
questions.explanation:
For \( Q_H=100 \) J: \( W=20 \) J, \( Q_C=80 \) J.

Reversed: \( \text{COP}=\dfrac{Q_C}{W}=\dfrac{80}{20}=4 \), i.e. \( \dfrac{1-\eta}{\eta} \).
questions.hint: Use numbers: take \( Q_H=100 \) J.
distractor_logic: This is \( 1/\eta=Q_H/W \), the heat-pump figure.
This is inverted.
This is \( 1-\eta \).

questions.topic: Reversible and Irreversible Processes, and the Carnot Engine
questions.question: A Carnot engine has efficiency \( 40\% \) with its sink at \( 300 \) K. By how much must the source temperature be raised to increase the efficiency to \( 50\% \), keeping the sink fixed?
questions.hint: Use \( T_H=\dfrac{T_C}{1-\eta} \) for both efficiencies.
distractor_logic: This assumes efficiency grows in simple proportion to \( T_H \).
This uses \( T_H=T_C/\eta \), which inverts the Carnot relation.
This is the source-sink gap \( T_H-T_C \), not the change needed.

questions.topic: Reversible and Irreversible Processes, and the Carnot Engine
questions.question: Two Carnot engines are in series between \( 800 \) K and \( 200 \) K: the first rejects heat at an intermediate temperature \( T \), which the second uses as its source. If both have equal efficiency, what is \( T \)?
questions.explanation:
Equal efficiency means \( \dfrac{T}{800}=\dfrac{200}{T} \).

\( T^{2}=160000 \), so \( T=400 \) K (each engine has \( 50\% \) efficiency).
questions.hint: Equal efficiency means equal temperature ratios.
distractor_logic: The arithmetic mean gives equal work, not equal efficiency.
This is the harmonic mean, which has no role here.
This is half the temperature difference, not a temperature in the range.

questions.topic: Reversible and Irreversible Processes, and the Carnot Engine
questions.question: A Carnot refrigerator removes \( 1000 \) J from a freezer at \( 250 \) K and releases heat into a room at \( 300 \) K. What is the minimum work required?
questions.hint: Find the COP from the temperatures.
distractor_logic: \( Q_C \) was multiplied by the COP.
This is \( Q_H \), the heat released to the room.
This assumes work equals heat removed.

questions.topic: Reversible and Irreversible Processes, and the Carnot Engine
questions.question: A Carnot engine between \( 500 \) K and \( 300 \) K absorbs \( 1000 \) J per cycle. All its work drives a Carnot refrigerator operating between \( 300 \) K and \( 250 \) K. How much heat does the refrigerator remove from the \( 250 \) K reservoir per cycle?
questions.explanation:
Engine: \( \eta=1-\dfrac{300}{500}=40\% \), so \( W=400 \) J.

Refrigerator: \( \text{COP}=\dfrac{250}{50}=5 \), so \( Q_C=5\times400=2000 \) J.
questions.hint: Engine gives work; refrigerator multiplies it by its COP.
distractor_logic: This is the work, not the heat removed.
The work was divided by the COP.
This is the heat the refrigerator releases at \( 300 \) K.

questions.topic: Reversible and Irreversible Processes, and the Carnot Engine
questions.question: One mole of ideal gas runs a Carnot cycle between \( 500 \) K and \( 300 \) K. In the isothermal expansion at \( 500 \) K the volume increases by a factor of \( e \). What is the net work done per cycle?
questions.explanation:
\( Q_H=RT_H\ln e=500R \). In a Carnot cycle the isothermal compression has the same volume ratio, so \( Q_C=300R \).

\( W=Q_H-Q_C=200R \).
questions.hint: Both isothermal legs have the same volume ratio.
distractor_logic: This is \( Q_H \), ignoring rejected heat.
The two heats were added.
This is \( Q_C \), the heat rejected.

questions.topic: Reversible and Irreversible Processes, and the Carnot Engine
questions.question: Which of these processes is reversible, at least in principle?
options: Heat conducted through a rod from a body at \( 400 \) K to one at \( 300 \) K
Slow isothermal expansion of an ideal gas with a frictionless piston, in contact with a reservoir at the same temperature
Two different gases mixing after a partition is removed
A gas rushing into a vacuum after a valve is opened
questions.explanation:
Reversibility needs quasi-static change with no friction and only infinitesimal temperature differences.

The slow frictionless isothermal expansion meets all three conditions; the others involve finite gradients or spontaneous mixing.
questions.hint: Look for slow, frictionless, and no finite temperature difference.

questions.question: An engine is placed between two reservoirs that are both at \( 350 \) K. How much net work can it deliver per cycle?
options: The most possible, since there are no losses
An amount set by the size of the reservoirs
questions.explanation:
Reservoirs at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium, so no net heat flows between them.

With \( T_C=T_H \), even the Carnot limit is \( 1-1=0 \).
questions.hint: Is there any temperature difference to exploit?
distractor_logic: Without a temperature difference there is nothing to run the engine.
Complete conversion of heat to work is forbidden in any case.
Size does not create a temperature difference.

questions.hint: The heat ratio equals the kelvin temperature ratio.

questions.question: A quasi-static process is one in which:
options: The system passes through a continuous series of equilibrium states
The change happens suddenly in a single step
No work is done by the system
questions.explanation:
A quasi-static process is so slow that the system has well-defined \( P \), \( V \), and \( T \) at every stage.

This is required for a process to be reversible and to be drawn as a curve on a P-V diagram.
questions.hint: Think of infinitely slow steps.
distractor_logic: Sudden changes pass through non-equilibrium states.
That is isothermal; quasi-static processes can change temperature.
Quasi-static expansions do work (area under the curve).

questions.question: A gas is used as the working substance of a refrigerator, and its cycle is traversed anticlockwise on a P-V diagram. The net work \( W \) done by the gas per cycle is:
options: Positive, equal to the enclosed area
Negative, with magnitude equal to the enclosed area
Zero, since the gas returns to its initial state
Negative, with magnitude equal to the area under the upper curve
questions.explanation:
Anticlockwise cycles give negative net work by the gas: work is done ON the gas.

Its magnitude is the enclosed area, which is the work input a refrigerator needs.
questions.hint: Direction sets the sign; enclosed area sets the size.
distractor_logic: Positive net work describes an engine (clockwise).
Returning to the start makes \( \Delta U \) zero, not \( W \).
Net work is the enclosed area, not the area under one curve.

questions.question: A Carnot engine using a monoatomic gas absorbs \( 1200 \) J at \( 600 \) K and rejects heat at \( 400 \) K. What are the work done and \( \Delta U \) of the gas over one complete cycle?
questions.explanation:
\( Q_C=1200\times\dfrac{400}{600}=800 \) J, so \( W=1200-800=400 \) J.

Over a full cycle the gas returns to its initial state, so \( \Delta U=0 \).
questions.hint: Use \( Q_C/Q_H=T_C/T_H \); a cycle has zero \( \Delta U \).
distractor_logic: Rejected heat leaves the gas; it is not stored as internal energy.
\( T_C/T_H \) was used as the efficiency.
This assumes \( 100\% \) efficiency.

questions.question: In which process does all the heat supplied go into internal energy, and in which does all of it go into work?
questions.explanation:
Isochoric: \( W=0 \), so \( Q=\Delta U \).

Isothermal (ideal gas): \( \Delta U=0 \), so \( Q=W \).
questions.hint: Which process has \( W=0 \), and which has \( \Delta U=0 \)?
distractor_logic: The two processes are swapped.
Isobaric splits heat between \( \Delta U \) and \( W \); adiabatic has no heat at all.
Adiabatic has \( Q=0 \), and isobaric always splits the heat.

questions.question: In a Carnot engine between \( 600 \) K and \( 300 \) K, the surroundings do \( 300 \) J of work on the gas during the isothermal compression at \( 300 \) K. What is the net work done by the gas per cycle?
questions.explanation:
Isothermal compression: \( \Delta U=0 \), so \( Q=W=-300 \) J, i.e. \( Q_C=300 \) J is rejected.

\( Q_H=Q_C\dfrac{T_H}{T_C}=600 \) J, so net \( W=Q_H-Q_C=300 \) J.
questions.hint: On an isothermal leg, heat equals work.
distractor_logic: This is \( Q_H \), ignoring the rejected heat.
The rejected heat was added to \( Q_H \).
Returning to the initial state makes \( \Delta U \) zero, not the net work.

questions.topic: The First Law of Thermodynamics and Specific Heat Capacities (Cp and Cv)
questions.question: When a bicycle pump is worked rapidly, the air inside the barrel becomes noticeably warmer. The best explanation is:
options: Compression is isothermal, so the air's internal energy stays constant
Rapid compression is nearly adiabatic, so the work done on the air raises its internal energy
Heat flows into the air from the cyclist's hand, making \( Q \) the main term
Compressing the air makes \( W \) positive, so \( \Delta U=Q-W \) increases
questions.explanation:
There is little time for heat to escape, so \( Q\approx0 \).

Work done on the air means \( W<0 \), so \( \Delta U=-W>0 \) and the temperature rises.
questions.hint: Fast processes have no time to exchange heat.
distractor_logic: If it were isothermal, the air would not warm up.
Heat from the hand is tiny compared with the work input in rapid pumping.
Compression makes work done by the gas negative; a positive \( W \) would lower \( \Delta U \).
